name: White noise machine

lead: A white noise machine plays steady broadband sound such as white, pink, or brown noise, fan sounds, or nature loops. People use it in noisy bedrooms to stay asleep through traffic, neighbors, and household noise, as a base for looking more rested.

Continuous sound reduces the contrast between background and sudden noises, so fewer arousals are triggered by the environment, and pink noise has also been studied for effects on slow-wave sleep. Results are mixed: a 2021 systematic review rated the quality of evidence for continuous noise as very low, while later reviews are more favorable in hospital settings.

paras: People play a steady sound from a small speaker or machine through the night, choosing a noise color or nature loop they find comfortable and keeping the device at a distance. It is used most in noisy bedrooms and for infants.

Playing it too loud may harm hearing; one paper found all 14 machines tested at maximum volume exceeded the 50 dB level considered safe for infants. Infant guidance stresses low volume and distance, and some people find the sound disruptive.

angle.text: Users play steady sound to mask noise so they wake less, treating uninterrupted sleep as the base for a more rested-looking face. Noise masking and sleep have been studied with mixed results; the appearance payoff comes through sleep quality.

lead: A white noise machine is a device that plays a steady, broadband sound intended to calm the listener or mask other noise. Despite the name, many such devices produce pink noise, whose power falls off at higher frequencies, or other noise colours or nature-like sounds, because true white noise sounds harsh [1]. They are used as sleep aids, for power-napping, for sound masking and privacy, and by some people with tinnitus [1].

In sleep-focused looksmaxxing, a machine is used to reduce wake-ups from traffic, neighbours or household noise, on the premise that better sleep supports appearance and recovery. Published evidence is mixed in scope: trials in hospital patients have reported improved sleep measures, while a 2024 scoping review raised concerns about continuous noise exposure in early childhood [2][3].

Volume is the main safety issue discussed in the literature. A paper cited by Wikipedia found that all 14 machines tested at maximum volume exceeded the 50 dB level considered safe for infants, and three exceeded the 85 dB adult threshold [1].

paras: Simple mechanical machines consist of an enclosed fan, sometimes with a speed switch, that pushes air through slots in the casing to make the sound; most modern units are electronic and play real-time generated or recorded audio [1]. Digital models often add Bluetooth, timers, volume limits and apps, and offer sounds such as rain, wind, ocean waves or traffic, sometimes blended with noise [1][4]. Electric fans are a common alternative; Wikipedia notes that some Asian communities historically avoided fans overnight because of a superstition about suffocation [1].

White noise has equal energy at every frequency, while pink noise, sometimes called 1/f noise, loses about 3 dB of energy per octave so each octave carries equal energy; it is often compared to the sound of a waterfall and is used to calibrate loudspeakers in professional audio.[5] Brown noise falls off more steeply. Wikipedia notes that most commercial 'white noise' machines actually produce pink noise or other colours, because true white noise sounds harsher.[1]
Digital machines often loop short recorded tracks, so the sound is not truly random, while fan-based units generate a continuous mechanical sound with an audible motor note.[1][4]

The Marpac Dohm, invented in 1962, is frequently credited as the original domestic fan-based white noise machine [1]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, attributes the first prototype to Rubbermaid executive James Buckwalter, who is said to have been inspired by a noisy motel stay, and to a 1964 patent for a sleep-inducing sound device filed with William Lahey and sold under Marpac brands [4]; that account has not been independently verified here. A 2017 Lancet Neurology historical note describes a seventeenth-century white noise machine associated with the sculptor Gian Lorenzo Bernini [6].

Wikipedia lists audio testing, sound masking, sleep aids and power napping, masking of tinnitus and privacy among the uses, and notes that specialised sound devices are used in managing insomnia and anxiety.[1] Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, adds focus and concentration, sensory support for autistic children, calming pets and travel use.[4] Privacy uses range from office sound masking to wearable devices intended to disrupt smart-speaker recording.[1]

The usual explanation is masking: a constant sound reduces the contrast between background and sudden noises, so sleepers are less likely to be roused by them [4]. Manufacturers of sound-masking devices recommend a comfortable starting volume, and manufacturers of sleep aids recommend a level slightly above normal music listening level but within a comfortable range [1].

sections.h: Reported effects on sleep and appearance
paras: The appearance case is a chain: a quieter-feeling bedroom may mean fewer awakenings, and consistent sleep is something skin, recovery and training routines depend on. Looksmaxxing sleep routines list machines next to blackout curtains, masks and cool rooms for that reason.[1] Hospital trials described below measured sleep scores and fatigue, not skin or looks.[2][7] Grokipedia says studies it cites link white noise to faster infant sleep onset and shorter adult sleep latency, and also says recent research suggests continuous noise may reduce REM or deep sleep for some people; both statements come from an AI-generated summary and are attributed here as such.[4]

A 2021 systematic review in Sleep Medicine Reviews examined noise as a sleep aid [8], and a 2022 systematic review in the Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine examined auditory stimulation and sleep [9]. Abstracts were not available to this article, so their detailed findings are not summarised here.

A randomized trial published in 2026 in a Taiwanese medical centre assigned 58 intensive care patients to white noise at 40 to 50 dB from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. for three nights or to routine care; the white noise group had greater reductions in total sleep scores and sleep disturbance and better sleep effectiveness on later days according to the Verran and Snyder-Halpern scale [2].

In a 2016 randomized trial of 120 hospitalised adults, all participants received an eye mask, earplugs and a white noise machine, and some also received education on their use. The educated group had a larger fall in fatigue scores, with trends toward improvement in other measures that were not statistically significant [7]. Because the tools were given together, the trial does not isolate the white noise machine.

A 2024 scoping review of 20 studies (seven animal, 13 paediatric, including 9,428 human subjects) on continuous white noise exposure during sleep and childhood development noted that machines can exceed 91 dB at maximum volume, reported deleterious effects of continuous moderate-intensity noise in animal models, and said human data generally agreed while also suggesting that low-intensity noise may be beneficial during sleep [3]. A cross-sectional 2026 survey of 253 parents at a paediatric otolaryngology clinic found 59.3 percent used white noise, mostly from a bedroom machine played overnight, mainly to improve sleep and to mask environmental noise [10].

The main concern is sound level, especially for infants. Wikipedia reports that machines tested at maximum volume exceeded recommended levels for babies, and some also exceeded adult occupational limits [1]. The scoping review's authors warned that white noise machines used incorrectly may be associated with poorer hearing, speech and learning outcomes in children [3]. Some adults find constant sound disruptive.

The 2014 Pediatrics study by Hugh and colleagues measured 14 infant sleep machines at maximum volume: at 30 cm every device exceeded 50 A-weighted dB, the recommended limit for hospital nurseries, and three exceeded 85 dB, beyond adult occupational limits for an 8-hour exposure; the authors concluded the machines could produce levels that may damage infant hearing and auditory development.[1] Grokipedia reports a recommendation that volume at an infant's location not exceed 50 dB with the machine placed about two metres (seven feet) from the crib.[4] Wikipedia notes there is little research on very loud or inaudible frequencies.[1]

Machines appear in sleep-environment routines alongside blackout curtains, masks and cooler rooms. Claims about appearance benefits rely on the indirect link between sleep and skin or recovery; white noise machines have not been studied for appearance outcomes.

Features commonly cited include a choice of sound types, a volume limiter, timers, battery or USB operation for travel, and non-looping audio. Prices usually range from about $20 to $50, with higher-end models around $100 [4]. Because of the volume findings above, maximum output level is a specification discussed in the research literature [1][3].
